profile.name: Yingge dance
profile.tagline: A vigorous Chinese folk dance fusing martial arts and Water Margin opera.
profile.insight: Originating in the mid-Ming dynasty, Yingge troupes deploy anywhere from 16 to 108 performers pounding drums and striking cudgels in a fierce rhythm without melody.
profile.profile: Yingge dance is a dynamic Chinese folk square dance originating in the mid-Ming dynasty within the Chaoshan region of Guangdong. Fusing Southern-style martial arts and Chinese opera, troupes of 16 to 108 performers bring outlaws from the Water Margin to life. Performers wield short cudgels or hand drums, executing precise striking patterns driven entirely by gongs and drums.
profile.profile_long:
Yingge dance is a traditional Chinese folk square dance that originated in the mid-Ming dynasty and is especially popular in the Chaopu-Huilu area, encompassing Chaoyang, Puning, Huilai, and Lufeng. The art form deeply integrates elements of Southern-style martial arts and Chinese opera into a unified local performance style. Historical records from the Qianlong era note early forms of Yangge in the region, while later Jiaqing and Daoguang periods saw strong influences from local theater dramas such as The Attack on Daming Prefecture. On May 20, 2006, Yingge was officially inscribed into the first list of China’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage. 

Performances are categorized by rhythm, tempo, and cudgel technique into Slow-tempo, Medium-tempo, and Fast-tempo styles. Slow-tempo Yingge features longer cudgels around 60 cm, simple rustic movements, and sets of three or four strikes without character face paint. Medium-tempo Yingge utilizes 57 cm cudgels and incorporates stances from Southern Fist martial arts. Fast-tempo Yingge uses the shortest cudgels, around 40 cm, emphasizing rapid, dynamic striking and retraction across styles like Jianshan and Nanshan.

A Yingge troupe's size depends on village manpower, always consisting of an even number between 16 and 108 members, commonly aligned with the Thirty-Six Heavenly Spirits or Seventy-Two Earthly Fiends. Performers wear striking facial makeup divided into ghost-face and opera-face styles, portraying heroes of the Water Margin. Lead roles include the red-faced First Hammer, black-faced Second Hammer, and the snake dancer representing Shi Qian. Costumes feature general helmets, hero robes, armor suits, and straw-soled shoes. The musical accompaniment is strictly percussive, consisting entirely of rhythm from bass drums, medium drums, gongs, cymbals, and shell horns without any melody.

sections.origins_and_history: Yingge Dance originated in the mid-Ming dynasty in the Chaoshan region of Guangdong, specifically in the Chaopu-Huilu area. Various origin theories exist, including relations to the Water Margin, Nuo rituals, and Waijiang Opera. Local gazetteers from the Qianlong era document early Yangge gatherings, and theatrical influences became prominent during the Jiaqing and Daoguang periods.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances involve 16 to 108 male dancers using even-numbered groupings. Dancers execute front stage routines involving cudgel strikes, hand drums, and formations driven by footwork and Southern Fist martial arts stances such as Da Zhan Ma.
sections.music_and_instruments: Yingge dance music consists solely of rhythm without melody. The percussion ensemble includes bass drums, medium drums, Qinzai copper gongs, big gongs, cymbals, cloud gongs, Nao bo water cymbals, conch horns, and ox horns.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear general helmets, Luo hats, straw hats, headscarfs, hero robes, exaggerated robes, armor suits, and straw-soled shoes. Facial makeup includes ghost-face and opera-face styles representing Water Margin outlaws, with performers often wearing full beards.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dances depict legendary outlaws from the Water Margin attacking Daming Prefecture to rescue Lu Junyi or Song Jiang. It was inscribed as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage item on May 20, 2006.
sections.notable_figures: Key roles include the First Hammer (Qin Ming or Guan Sheng), Second Hammer (Li Kui), Third Hammer (Lu Zhishen), Fourth Hammer (Wu Song), Shi Qian (snake dancer), Song Jiang or Lin Chong as drummers, and Gongsun Sheng carrying a command flag.
sections.regional_variants: Classified into Slow-tempo Yingge (longer cudgels, Miancheng), Medium-tempo Yingge (Southern Fist stances), and Fast-tempo Yingge (shortest cudgels, including Jianshan, Nanshan Wen, Nanshan Wu, and paired-combat styles).
sections.lineage: Derived from a synthesis of Southern-style martial arts, Chinese opera, and traditional Yangge folk gatherings.

music_profile.musical_form: consists only of rhythm, without melody
music_profile.sound_description: A powerful percussive wall of sound driven by bass and medium drums, copper gongs, cymbals, and shell horns, completely devoid of melody.

movement_profile.footwork: footwork being the most important as it drives all other techniques

movement_profile.formation_and_space: forming and transforming various formations to form various patterns

signature_moves.description: Striking wooden Yingge cudgels in rhythm with gongs and drums

episode_brief.title_hook: The Thunder of Chaoshan: Inside the Yingge Dance
episode_brief.logline: Armed with cudgels and warrior face paint, a troupe of dancers brings Water Margin legends to life through pure percussion.
beats: Introduction to the Chaoshan region and mid-Ming origins.
The integration of Southern-style martial arts and Chinese opera.
Applying the head scarf and traditional opera face paint.
The percussive wall of sound from bass drums and gongs without melody.
Comparing slow, medium, and fast tempo cudgel styles.
The grand formation of the Thirty-Six Heavenly Spirits.
A full front stage performance depicting the attack on Daming Prefecture.
